newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.C. MAC seen backing infrastructure agency plan.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.C. MAC seen backing infrastructure agency plan.

text.p: The Municipal Assistance Corp (MAC) of New York City likely will support a controversial plan to sidestep the city's debt limit by creating a new infrastructure authority, a MAC official said on Friday.
"My feeling is that it makes a lot of sense and I think that is the feeling the board will express," Quentin Spector, the executive director, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

The MAC board on Monday holds its annual meeting in New York City, at which it is also plans to discuss the performance of the cap on operating expenses that it agreed with the city and take up prompt payment and annual reports.

Spector noted that the board is unlikely to issue a statement supporting the new infrastructure agency proposed by the Giuliani Administration or approve a resolution backing the plan because it has yet to see a formal outline.

While a draft version of a bill that would create such a new agency has been completed, a city source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said that it still is being reviewed and might be altered before it is sent to Albany.

The state legislature would have to approve of such a new agency, and city officials are considering submitting their bill this autumn, as Gov. George Pataki has said he plans to recall the legislature after the November 5 elections.
The special session likely will be needed to deal with the sweeping changes required by the new federal welfare reforms.
New York City's constitutional debt limit is $33 billion, and as it now has around $30 billion of outstanding obligations, it is expected to reach the limit in 1998.
The New York state and city comptrollers have said the plan for the new infrastructure authority raised numerous concerns.

The Giuliani Administration has proposed that the Authority, which would issue debt that was backed by the city's personal income tax revenues, would fund education, transit and transportation capital projects.
In its four-year plan, the Administration suggested that the agency issue $3.4 billion of debt, starting in fiscal year 1998.
